newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Spain August CPI seen spiking higher.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Spain August CPI seen spiking higher.

text.p: Spain's consumer inflation in August was likely to have been bloated by emergency government tax measures, but analysts said the blip would not threaten long-term price moderation.

Economists polled by Reuters forecast that inflation, due to be announced on Friday, was 0.5 percent month-on-month in August, for a 3.9 percent year-on-year rate. In July, prices rose 0.1 and 3.7 percent respectively.

"The market is looking beyond the (August) number. It sees fresh food continuing to fall and it is also aware that the rigidity in the price-regulated sector is declining," an analyst at a major Spanish bank said.

The range of forecasts in the Reuter survey was for a month-on-month rise of 0.3 to 0.6 percent, or a year-on-year rise of 3.7 to 4.0 percent. On average, core inflation is seen having risen 0.30 percent or 3.7 percent.
"Service sector prices are growing at a relatively stable rate, while industrial goods inflation is on a clear downward trend," said Bank of America in a brokers note.

The August data will be hit by an emergency rise at the start of last month in tobacco and alcohol taxes. The government levied the additional taxes to plug a gap of 721 billion pesetas left over from the 1995 budget.
At first, experts said the measure could push prices two-tenths of a percentage point higher in August, but many have since softened these predictions.
"The impact of the tobacco tax rise hasn't been that substantial. It has been greater in alcohol," said an economist at a commercial bank's research department.
Market leader Tabacalera did not pass on the full cigarette tax rise to its customers.
Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro told parliament on Wednesday there were "positive signs" on August inflation.

Bond market specialists said a more modest than forecast month-on-month rise could lend credibility to the government's official projection of inflation ending the year at 3.4 percent after 4.3 percent in 1995.

"If it comes out under (0.5 percent) the market could rebound. It is important to highlight that a possible spike in CPI would be due to seasonal factors," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, Bank of America analyst.
But an in line forecast could prompt a wave of profit-taking, said Santiago Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais.
